Myositis Ossificans: Did the Pain Resolve and Come Back?

Heterotopic bone weeks after a contusion; does passive stretch reproduce the pain?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A contusion whose pain clears, then returns weeks later with a firm, mobile intramuscular mass, is myositis ossificans: bone forming inside the muscle (quadriceps and brachialis most often).

The exam decides it:

  • Pain on passive stretch of the muscle (knee flexion for the quadriceps)
  • Strength and sensation intact
  • No fever, erythema or limb-wide swelling

Early films are often normal; calcification appears at about 4 to 8 weeks. Never biopsy an early lesion: it can mimic osteosarcoma.

Treat with range of motion and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) such as indomethacin; excise only a mature lesion that stays symptomatic.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Lesion – lamellar bone in muscle (heterotopic ossification) · Trigger – muscle injury, fracture or surgery such as arthroplasty; or neurologic: stroke, brain or spinal cord injury · Labs – alkaline phosphatase, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) may rise, so they do not exclude infection
Mimics the stem rules out Quadriceps tendon tear – knee extension lost, gap above the patella · Venous thrombosis – whole thigh and calf swollen; 2 cm more thigh girth alone is not enough · Osteoid osteoma – night pain relieved by NSAIDs, no mass
Management and treatment
Management ladder: myositis ossificans
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineRange of motion and an NSAID; no forceful stretching or deep massageStill painful and limited with a mature lesion after at least 6 to 12 months
SurgeryExcise the mature lesion completely; early excision recursTop rung
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy, football thigh contusion 4 weeks ago pain gone by 2 weeks, back last week indurated, mobile 3-cm anterior mass; no erythema passive knee flexion hurts; strength, sensation normal Vital signs normal · thigh girth +2 cm · pulses, calves normal → Myositis ossificans → injury, recovery, then pain with a mobile intramuscular mass weeks later, hurt by stretching the muscle: heterotopic bone; no fever or erythema rules out infection, and a tumor progresses with night pain and never clears first
  2. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with myositis ossificans of the quadriceps today kicked in the thigh 4 weeks ago firm mass; knee flexion limited to 90 degrees Pain limits running Afebrile · radiograph: peripheral calcification → Range-of-motion exercise with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug → range of motion and an NSAID such as indomethacin; excision only for a mature lesion that stays symptomatic
  3. 15-year-old girl with a firm thigh mass 3 weeks after a soccer collision mass unchanged in size over 1 week pain on passive knee flexion No night pain, weight loss or fever Vital signs normal · radiograph of the thigh normal → Repeat imaging in 2 to 4 weeks → early films are often normal; repeat in 2 to 4 weeks to see peripheral calcification, since a biopsy of an immature lesion can mimic osteosarcoma
  4. 16-year-old boy with 1 day of severe thigh pain after a minor scrape spreading erythema and swelling pain out of proportion to the examination Confused and ill appearing T 39.0 °C · HR 128/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg → Emergency surgical exploration with broad-spectrum antibiotics → fever, spreading erythema and pain out of proportion within a day: necrotizing infection; operate now with broad antibiotics
  5. 45-year-old man who stumbled on stairs, landing on a flexed knee cannot extend the knee against gravity palpable gap just above the patella No induration or mass Sensation normal · knee radiograph: low-lying patella → Orthopedic referral for surgical repair → lost knee extension with a gap above the patella is a complete quadriceps tendon tear: surgical repair; a heterotopic mass leaves strength intact
  6. 24-year-old man 8 weeks after a traumatic brain injury stiff, painful right hip hard mass near the joint No fall or new injury since admission Afebrile · white cell count normal · alkaline phosphatase elevated → Neurogenic heterotopic ossification → the same heterotopic bone with a neurologic trigger (brain or spinal cord injury, stroke) and no trauma to the joint
  7. 18-year-old man with quadriceps myositis ossificans diagnosed 12 months ago still painful; knee flexion limited despite range-of-motion therapy and NSAIDs Mass unchanged for 6 months Afebrile · radiograph: mature, well-defined bone → Surgical excision → a mature lesion that stays symptomatic is excised; excising it before it matures invites recurrence
  8. 15-year-old boy was diagnosed with quadriceps myositis ossificans this week thigh contusion 3 weeks ago firm, tender anterior mass Asks how to speed recovery before the season Afebrile · knee flexion to 100 degrees → Aggressive passive stretching and deep massage of the lesion → aggressive passive stretching and deep massage of the lesion worsen the ossification; keep gentle active motion and an NSAID

Transferable rule

When a mass follows an injury, ask whether the pain cleared and came back, and what provokes it: stretch points to muscle, night pain to bone.
